December 26
Christmas 1C — The First Sunday of Christmas
Colors: white, gold
Isaiah 61:10-end, 62:1-5
Psalm 147:13-21
Gal 3:23-4:7
Jn 1:1-18
"The First Sunday of Christmas"
Grace and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, creator of all that is and giver of life.

The Gospel of John has been described as the Pearl of Great Price within the Bible. Raymond Brown, author of my favorite commentary on The Gospel of John, describes the first 18 verses (John 1:1-18) as the Pearl of Great Price within the Pearl of Great Price.

It is overloaded with information about who Jesus is. This makes it somewhat difficult to come to grips with. I think it is fair to say many a Biblical Scholar has made his career writing about these verses. There is a lot of debate about who wrote what, when, and what about. When I was studying this section what came to mind was n-dimensional vectors. And I don't suppose that would help anyone but me, and even then, not that much. Suffice it to say this section is more complex than most.

That being said, we do not have to know there are 1.5 septillion molecules in a drop of water to enjoy a nice hot shower or that you have to be a Biblical Scholar to learn from these 18 verses.

I think it helps to remember why St. John wrote this. At the end of the 20th chapter, he says, "These are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name." These verses are written so that you might have the life that dwells in Jesus and is his to give away.

One of the things we learn in these opening verses of John's Gospel is that everything is created by the Word.

I suppose I should stop here and explain that when St. John says *the Word,* he is referring to Jesus before Jesus was born. In theological language, we say *the pre-incarnate Jesus*. I have read a handful of arguments about the differences between the pre- and post- incarnate Jesus and am grateful to a Roman Catholic theologian who said he's not sure it makes a wit of difference. For the sake of simplicity, I am just going to refer the *the Word* as Jesus (if you want to quibble, we can talk later).

So, Jesus creates everything. And St. John wants to make extra-special-sure that we get that. He says, "All things were made through him," then adds,  "and without him was not any thing made that was made." There is just no wiggle room here. If it's here, Jesus made it.

This has some amazing implications. If you look at something, anything, that thing has the unmistakable stamp, *made by Jesus.* St. Paul tells us, "For what can be known about God is plain to [everyone], because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made..." (Romans 1:19-20).

Of course, it might take a geologist to look at a rock and say, "Whoa! Jesus has been busy!" Still, most people have had an experience of a walk in a forest, looking at a sunset, seeing a newborn baby, and possibly, for some peculiar people (not naming names), a steam locomotive and had the feeling that Jesus has been hard at work.

None of these things, and not to mention a host of others, are not God or even contain little tiny bits of God - and when I say God here, I mean Jesus. What they do contain is the unmistakable imprint of his action, the mark saying, "Jesus made this." One of the questions we should be asking ourselves is, *are we looking for that mark?* Paraphrasing St. Paul - it's there if we are willing to look. One of the difficulties we people have is our unwillingness to look for the maker's mark on the things of Creation.

There is more to Jesus' creative efforts than just stuff. St. John carries on in the 4th & 5th verses, "In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it." What he seems to be telling us is that thing that is *life*, whatever life technically is, resides in Jesus. We can infer that without Jesus there would only be stuff and not life.

That life contained in Jesus, he shares with us. St. John's way of saying that is, "the life was the light of men." The very thing that separates us from stuff is the life Jesus shares with us. It lights us up and distinguishes us from stuff. This life and light Jesus shares with us is unmistakable in that no amount of darkness is able to hide or overcome its brightness. We are not talking about a small candle here, but light so bright there is nothing able to cast a shadow. There is no hiding from the life and light of Jesus.

Even so, St. John needs to remind us, "The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him." This is an astonishing thing. The maker of the world, the one who shares his life with the world, comes into the world he made, and the response of the world isn't even, "What do you want?" but more along the lines of, "I am sort of busy here, would mind getting out of my way?"

We are a tough crowd.

Being a tough crowd is not the end of the story. Referring back to the 20th chapter of John again, "these are written so that you may [trust] that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by [trusting] you may have life in his name." Back at the 12th verse of what we read this morning we hear all who welcomed Jesus, who trusted him, Jesus gave them the right to become children of God. As children of God, brothers and sisters of Jesus, we carry in us the life of Jesus, which is light to all. The life and light of Jesus is a gift to be cherished and shared.

The peace of God, which passes all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in the knowledge and love of God, and of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord; and the blessing of God Almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, be among you, and remain with you always.
paul+
